title: Ch. 1 — Quoting the Ancestors
paragraphs: The chapter's epigraph is Archytas: place is the first of all beings, since everything that exists is in a place and cannot exist without a place. What follows is Basso in a Jeep and on horseback with Charles Henry and Morley Cromwell, learning that the claim is not decorative.

At the first stop he meets his own incompetence. Trying to record the name of a seep where clay-clouded water stands in a natural basin, he mangles it, and proposes to come back to it later. Charles Henry declines to move on, and repeats it patiently until Basso gets it: Water Lies With Mud In An Open Container. What he had not foreseen was that his hurry would be read as disrespect — because to speak an Apache place-name is to repeat, word for word, the speech of the ancestors who conferred it. In the ancestral scene Charles builds, a leader judges that the place might let his people survive and says they must name it in order to speak of it and remember it well. They made a picture of it with words.

Then the names begin to teach other things. At Snakes' Water, the spring is dry and hidden behind manzanita, and Charles points out the lack of match between the place and the name. Many names, he says, record springs, seeps and bogs that are now permanently dry — Birds' Water, Foul Water. Yet the names are kept, because they are faithful photographs of the land as the ancestors found it: the names do not lie, he insists, they show what is different and what is still the same. In the story he tells, the people are forbidden to approach until a man who knows how to speak to the snakes has asked them to move aside; when the water is gone, the women wail as if a relative had died, and everyone prays for Water to take pity.

At Juniper Tree Stands Alone the pattern turns social. The ancestors who first planted corn on that flat took the name of the place as the name of themselves, becoming Juniper Tree Stands Alone People — and the clan still plants the same fields. Ellen Josay Tessay, its oldest member, settles on a ground cloth and pulls weeds; told she is helping her corn, she answers that she is looking after her children. This is the middle of the three naming layers Charles is teaching: descriptive names came first, while the ancestors were exploring and deciding to stay; clan names were built from them once people had gathered near farms; commemorative names came last, once the land was theirs and community life had produced both rewards and painful problems.

The commemorative layer is where the landscape acquires a conscience, and the chapter's darkest name shows how. At Shades Of Shit, people with ample corn refused their starving relatives, and the hungry kin penned them inside their own brush shelters until they were living in their own filth and close to death. The reproach is not about manners: as relatives we make each other rich because we help each other in times of need, and it has been that way since the beginning. Charles finds the received story threadbare and enlarges it, building the place-world with obvious skill — because place-making is a way of constructing history, of inventing it, and Basso concludes that we are, in a sense, the place-worlds we imagine.

Two smaller stops fill in the method. At Bitter Agave Plain and Scattered Rocks Stand Erect, Charles slips into the past and lets the ancestors speak in the present tense, marvelling at seed-heavy grass and wondering, half afraid, why the rocks stand as they do. Apache place-making, Basso says, is a form of narrative art — historical theatre in which the pastness of the past is stripped away, thick with quoted speech, concise and closely plotted, whose themes are survival, the importance of kin, and the benefits of adhering to moral norms. Edward Spicer complained in 1962 that no Apache chronicler had emerged. This chapter is the answer: the chronicling never stopped, it simply was never written down.
